intro.title: The Girl in the Photograph
p: The first time you saw the girl in the photograph, she was standing beside your grandmother.
The second time, she was standing alone.
You discovered the difference three weeks after the funeral. The picture had been hidden between the pages of an old cookbook.
The photograph was dated June 14th, 1987. Your grandmother was twenty-six. The girl beside her looked exactly like you.
On the back, your grandmother had written: If she comes looking for you, do not tell her your name.
At that exact moment, the telephone rang.
“I am calling about the house,” a woman said. “Has anyone opened the upstairs room?”
Behind her voice, someone was humming a lullaby you remembered from childhood.
“Why the upstairs room?”
The woman hesitated. “Because it was sealed twenty-nine years ago. And someone opened it last night.”
The call ended.
“Who is singing?”
The melody stopped. A second voice whispered into the receiver: “She can hear us.”
The call ended.
Something slid beneath your apartment door.
A cream-coloured envelope. No footsteps followed it. Across the front, in your grandmother’s handwriting: FOR THE ONE WHO STAYED.
The wax seal showed a small bird surrounded by seven stars.
choices: Hold the envelope against the lamp

p: The wax cracked beneath your thumb.
Inside, a letter: “There were two of you that summer. But only one came home.”
A tiny brass key was taped beneath the final line.
You held the envelope close to the lamp. The paper slowly turned translucent.
A hidden sentence emerged: “She is not your sister. She is what the house kept.”
You lowered the letter. The words were gone.
The photograph lay on your desk.
Three quiet knocks sounded at the window. You lived on the fifth floor.
The girl in the photograph was no longer looking at your grandmother. She was looking at you.
Beyond the glass, the night was empty.
Then a handprint appeared on the outside of the window. Five perfectly ordinary fingers.
Underneath, a word formed in the condensation: COME.
You turned the photograph over.
The warning was gone. A new message had appeared in the same handwriting: “You remember me, don’t you?”
The paper felt warm against your palm.

end.title: The House Is Waiting
p: By morning, you knew you would return to the house.
Your grandmother had not been trying to keep you away from it.
She had been trying to keep something inside.
